record.paper_title: Open problems on graphs arising from geometric topology
record.original_question: Let K be a tree embedded in the Euclidean plane R^2 and let epsilon be positive. Say that K is genuinely epsilon-disjoinable if there is a continuous or piecewise-linear map f: K -> R^2 such that K and f(K) are disjoint and every point x of K moves by less than epsilon, |x - f(x)| < epsilon. Say that K is epsilon-spanned if two closed round disks of diameter epsilon, whose centers move continuously on K and are never allowed to intersect, cannot be moved so that their two traces on K become the same. Say that K is symmetrically epsilon-spanned if such disks cannot exchange their positions. Does genuine epsilon-disjoinability imply epsilon-spannedness, and does symmetric epsilon-spannedness imply epsilon-spannedness for plane trees?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a tree (a compact, connected, simply connected $1$-dimensional polyhedron) embedded in the Euclidean plane, and let $\varepsilon > 0$.

(i) Call $K$ genuinely $\varepsilon$-disjoinable if there exists a continuous (equivalently, piecewise-linear) map $f \colon K \to \mathbb{R}^2$ such that $f(K) \cap K = \emptyset$ and $|x - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in K$.

(ii) Consider two closed round disks $D_1, D_2 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, each of diameter $\varepsilon$, whose centers $c_1(t), c_2(t)$ move continuously along $K$ as functions of $t \in [0,1]$, and which are required to remain disjoint at every time $t$ (that is, $D_1(t) \cap D_2(t) = \emptyset$ for all $t$). The trace of $D_i$ on $K$ at time $t$ is the set $D_i(t) \cap K$. Call $K$ $\varepsilon$-spanned if there is no such admissible motion of the two disks that results in their two traces on $K$ coinciding at the end (i.e.\ one cannot move the disks so that, at some time, $D_1(t) \cap K = D_2(t) \cap K$ as subsets of $K$). Call $K$ symmetrically $\varepsilon$-spanned if no such admissible motion exchanges the disks (i.e.\ achieves $(c_1(1), c_2(1)) = (c_2(0), c_1(0))$).

Answer the following:

(a) Does genuine $\varepsilon$-disjoinability of $K$ imply that $K$ is $\varepsilon$-spanned?

(b) Does symmetric $\varepsilon$-spannedness of $K$ imply that $K$ is $\varepsilon$-spanned?
